topics.label: AI Literacy & Capability
topics.description: Critical capabilities needed to become AI fluent — frameworks, competencies, and workforce readiness.

articles.title: A competency framework for digital public health in Europe: an updated scoping review | npj Digital Public Health - Nature
articles.snippet: A competency framework for digital public health in Europe: an updated scoping review | npj Digital Public Health  Nature
articles.generalisability: Moderate — focused on European public health context; competency frameworks may have limited direct applicability to Australian organisational settings outside healthcare, though core digital literacy principles may transfer.
takeaways: Identify which digital competencies are most critical for your workforce by reviewing what public health systems across Europe have prioritised—this can inform your own AI literacy curriculum design.
Consider adopting a structured competency framework approach (rather than ad-hoc training) to systematically map skill gaps and progression levels in AI capabilities across your organisation.
European frameworks may emphasise regulatory compliance and ethical oversight; ensure your Australian context incorporates relevant local data governance and risk management standards.

articles.title: From resistance to readiness: faculty development as the key to AI literacy in public health - Frontiers
articles.snippet: From resistance to readiness: faculty development as the key to AI literacy in public health  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Limited — appears focused on public health faculty development context; applicability to other sectors or non-academic settings unclear without full article review.
takeaways: Design faculty development programs that address resistance to AI adoption by building confidence and competence before expecting uptake of AI tools in teaching or practice.
Position AI literacy training as an ongoing developmental pathway rather than a one-off compliance requirement to shift staff mindsets from resistance to readiness.
Create structured faculty development opportunities that model how to integrate AI literacy into curricula, giving educators practical experience before they teach it to students.

articles.title: Integration of artificial intelligence competencies into a holistic digital literacy framework for middle school education - Nature
articles.snippet: Integration of artificial intelligence competencies into a holistic digital literacy framework for middle school education  Nature
articles.generalisability: Unclear from snippet — appears to propose a conceptual framework for middle school AI literacy, but geographic scope and empirical validation are not evident. Findings may be most relevant to secondary education contexts.
takeaways: Consider how AI competencies map to existing digital literacy frameworks in your organisation rather than treating AI as a standalone capability — integration is more effective than siloed training.
Identify which AI competencies are foundational (e.g., understanding bias, data basics) versus advanced, so you can scaffold learning pathways for mixed-experience cohorts.

articles.title: Strategies for developing AI competencies in higher education - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Strategies for developing AI competencies in higher education  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Moderate — focuses on higher education context, which may not directly transfer to corporate workplace settings. Geographic scope unclear from snippet provided.
takeaways: Identify which AI competencies are most critical for your employees' roles, then design targeted upskilling programmes rather than generic AI awareness training.
Create structured learning pathways that progress from foundational AI literacy to role-specific application, mirroring approaches successfully used in university settings.
Integrate hands-on, practical AI projects into learning to build confidence and real-world competency, not just conceptual understanding.

articles.title: AI literacy as a meta-skill: a four-domain model for academic management innovation in higher education - Frontiers
articles.snippet: AI literacy as a meta-skill: a four-domain model for academic management innovation in higher education  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Moderate — focuses on higher education context, which has distinct organisational structures and workforce characteristics compared to corporate or government sectors. Applicability to non-academic organisations would require adaptation.
takeaways: Consider framing AI literacy as a foundational meta-skill rather than isolated technical training; design programs around interconnected domains rather than standalone modules to increase transfer across roles and contexts.

For academic managers specifically, identify which of the four domains (likely technical understanding, strategic thinking, ethical reasoning, and change management) are most critical to your institution's priorities, then sequence development accordingly rather than treating all domains equally.

Use this framework to audit existing leadership development programs in your organisation — assess which domains are currently underdeveloped and create targeted interventions to close gaps in manager capability.

articles.title: AI literacy in undergraduate medical education: a competency-based interpretive framework for curriculum and assessment - Frontiers
articles.snippet: AI literacy in undergraduate medical education: a competency-based interpretive framework for curriculum and assessment  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Moderate — focuses on undergraduate medical education specifically; the competency framework may apply to other health professions and professional education, but direct applicability to non-medical contexts would require adaptation.
takeaways: Develop a competency-based framework for AI literacy that maps specific skills and knowledge to curriculum design and assessment methods — this approach can be adapted for any professional training programme requiring AI capability development.
Use interpretive frameworks to define what AI literacy means in your discipline before rolling out training; this helps clarify which capabilities matter most and how to measure them credibly.
Design assessment methods that align with competencies rather than content coverage alone — this ensures employees can demonstrate practical AI capability relevant to their role.

topics.label: AI & Organisational Psychology
topics.description: Impact of AI on wellbeing, engagement, job crafting, trust, and other org psych constructs.

articles.title: The double-edged mechanism of organizational AI adoption on employee creativity - Frontiers
articles.snippet: The double-edged mechanism of organizational AI adoption on employee creativity  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability unclear without access to full article — depends on sample size, organisational sectors studied, and geographic scope. The 'double-edged' framing suggests contextual factors matter significantly for outcomes.
takeaways: AI adoption can both enhance and inhibit employee creativity depending on implementation approach — assess whether your rollout emphasizes augmentation (AI as creative tool) versus automation (AI replacing creative work).
Monitor psychological and motivational responses during AI adoption; negative effects on creativity may stem from perceived job threat or loss of autonomy rather than AI capability limitations.
Design AI integration with deliberate attention to preserving creative problem-solving space — avoid over-automating tasks that develop employee skills and confidence in their creative contribution.

articles.title: Work autonomy mediates associations between medical AI readiness and well being in a three wave nurse study - Nature
articles.snippet: Work autonomy mediates associations between medical AI readiness and well being in a three wave nurse study  Nature
articles.generalisability: Findings are specific to nursing contexts and may not generalise to other professional groups. The three-wave longitudinal design strengthens causal inference, but geographic scope and sample size are unclear from the snippet.
takeaways: Preserving worker autonomy is critical when introducing AI tools — the relationship between AI readiness and employee wellbeing depends on whether staff retain control over how they use the technology.

During AI implementation in healthcare settings, assess and protect clinical autonomy alongside technical readiness; loss of autonomy may undermine wellbeing gains even if staff are prepared for the technology.
Design AI adoption programmes that explicitly maintain or expand clinician decision-making authority rather than centralising decisions or automating judgement calls without staff input.

articles.title: Competing strain and resource pathways linking AI-enabled work systems to employee wellbeing - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Competing strain and resource pathways linking AI-enabled work systems to employee wellbeing  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on sample composition — typically limited until full article reviewed, but the theoretical framework of competing strain/resource pathways has broad applicability to AI-augmented work contexts across sectors.
takeaways: AI systems can simultaneously create workload strain (e.g. additional monitoring, upskilling demands) and provide resources (e.g. task automation, decision support) — your intervention design should address both pathways to avoid net negative wellbeing outcomes.

When implementing AI-enabled systems, assess and mitigate strain triggers (job demands, role ambiguity, loss of autonomy) while actively building resource buffers (training, autonomy in AI use, psychological safety) to maximise employee wellbeing.

articles.title: Dual pathways of generative AI use: role ambiguity and self-efficacy in employee-AI collaboration - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Dual pathways of generative AI use: role ambiguity and self-efficacy in employee-AI collaboration  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Cannot assess from title and snippet alone — generalisability depends on sample composition, sector coverage, and geographic scope, which are not provided in the available information.
takeaways: Role ambiguity about how to use AI in your job can be addressed through clear task-AI fit guidelines and explicit protocols — organisations should define when and how teams should collaborate with AI tools rather than leaving adoption ad hoc.

Self-efficacy (confidence in using AI) is a lever you can strengthen through targeted training, peer modelling, and low-stakes practice opportunities — employees who feel capable of using AI tools are more likely to adopt them productively.

These two factors (clarity of role + confidence in capability) interact — even well-trained employees may underutilise AI if unclear about their responsibilities, so pair capability-building with role-design interventions.

articles.title: When AI works, employees worry: the vigilance cost of AI delegation in hybrid work - Frontiers
articles.snippet: When AI works, employees worry: the vigilance cost of AI delegation in hybrid work  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on study design and sample characteristics not evident from title/snippet. Findings may be most applicable to hybrid work settings, but geographic scope and sector representation unclear.
takeaways: When delegating tasks to AI in hybrid work, expect employees to experience increased cognitive load from monitoring AI outputs — plan for this 'vigilance cost' by building in review time and support rather than assuming AI delegation reduces workload

Hybrid work settings may amplify concern about AI reliability when oversight is remote; consider establishing clear protocols for AI-assisted work and regular check-ins to address employee anxiety about delegated tasks

articles.title: Organizational psychological ownership drives employee-AI collaboration via AI crafting under paternalistic leadership - Nature
articles.snippet: Organizational psychological ownership drives employee-AI collaboration via AI crafting under paternalistic leadership  Nature
articles.generalisability: Unclear from snippet alone, but findings on paternalistic leadership may be more applicable in cultures where this management style is prevalent (e.g., East Asia) than in individualistic Western contexts like Australia.
takeaways: Foster psychological ownership of AI tools among employees — those who feel a sense of belonging and stake in AI systems are more likely to collaborate effectively with them rather than resist adoption.

In paternalistic leadership contexts, frame AI implementation as a collective endeavour where leaders guide and support employees' customisation of tools to their needs (AI crafting), rather than imposing standardised systems top-down.

Consider how your organisational culture and leadership style interact with AI adoption; the psychological mechanisms that drive collaboration may differ depending on whether your environment emphasises autonomy or guidance.

topics.label: Behavioural Change Frameworks
topics.description: Evidence-based frameworks for driving behaviour change — in the context of AI adoption and workforce transformation.

articles.title: AI adoption to adaptation: How a new change approach can build the human behaviors needed for AI - Deloitte
articles.snippet: AI adoption to adaptation: How a new change approach can build the human behaviors needed for AI  Deloitte
articles.generalisability: Moderate — Deloitte's practitioner insights are informed by consulting experience but lack specific data on sample size, sectors, or geographies. Findings may reflect practices primarily in large enterprise environments.
takeaways: Shift your change strategy from 'AI adoption' (implementing tools) to 'AI adaptation' (building new human behaviours and mindsets) — this reframing helps identify what skills, workflows, and cultural shifts your team actually needs to develop.
Design behaviour change interventions that target the specific human capabilities required for your AI use cases, rather than focusing solely on system deployment or feature rollout.
Structure your change approach to address both technical readiness and human readiness in parallel — adoption failures often stem from underestimating the behaviour change work required.

articles.title: How AI Is Reshaping the Future of Work - Stanford Graduate School of Business
articles.snippet: How AI Is Reshaping the Future of Work  Stanford Graduate School of Business
articles.generalisability: Limited — appears to be a perspective piece from Stanford GSB without specified empirical scope. Findings and recommendations may reflect US business education context and may not directly transfer to Australian organisational settings.
takeaways: Identify specific work processes in your organisation where AI adoption is reshaping roles, then proactively communicate changes to employees to reduce uncertainty and resistance.
Design transition support (retraining, role clarity, career pathways) before implementing AI tools, rather than after — this reduces anxiety and improves change adoption rates.
Engage employees early in AI implementation conversations to gather frontline insights on practical barriers and opportunities, increasing buy-in and successful behaviour change.

articles.title: From adoption to impact: Three horizons of AI transformation - McKinsey & Company
articles.snippet: From adoption to impact: Three horizons of AI transformation  McKinsey & Company
articles.generalisability: Moderate — based on McKinsey's client work and industry surveys, but skewed toward large enterprises and may not reflect small-to-medium business contexts or non-English-speaking markets.
takeaways: Map your organization's AI transformation across three distinct phases (adoption, scaling, impact) to identify which horizon you're currently in and what behavioral and structural changes are needed to progress to the next phase.

Design change management strategies that address the specific adoption barriers and capability gaps relevant to your organization's horizon — early-stage teams need different support (upskilling, psychological safety) than scaling or impact-focused teams.
Establish clear metrics and feedback loops at each horizon to sustain momentum and demonstrate value to stakeholders, helping maintain employee engagement and buy-in through visible progress.

articles.title: Are all digital hoarding behavior alike? Uncovering the pathways to digital hoarding behavior in the workplace - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Are all digital hoarding behavior alike? Uncovering the pathways to digital hoarding behavior in the workplace  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Limited — without access to full article, geographic scope and sample characteristics are unclear. Findings on workplace digital hoarding pathways may vary across organisational cultures and technology maturity levels.
takeaways: Recognise that digital hoarding (excessive file retention, duplicate storage) likely stems from multiple distinct behavioural pathways — not a single cause — requiring tailored intervention strategies rather than one-size-fits-all solutions.

Use pathway analysis to diagnose whether employees hoard digitally due to uncertainty/risk aversion, lack of trust in retrieval systems, or unclear data governance — then design targeted behaviour-change interventions (e.g. trust-building for system reliability vs. clear deletion protocols for risk-averse staff).

articles.title: Dual-path mechanism of AI awareness on employee job crafting: insights from the cognitive appraisal of stress and JD-R perspective | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications - Nature
articles.snippet: Dual-path mechanism of AI awareness on employee job crafting: insights from the cognitive appraisal of stress and JD-R perspective | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications  Nature
articles.generalisability: Generalisability unclear from snippet alone; likely limited by undisclosed sample characteristics (sector, geography, organisational type). Findings based on cognitive appraisal theory and Job Demands-Resources framework are conceptually sound, but empirical scope and representativeness cannot be assessed without full methodology.
takeaways: Employee responses to AI awareness operate through two distinct cognitive pathways—stress appraisal and resource evaluation—meaning interventions should address both threat perception and opportunity recognition rather than assuming uniform change.

Job crafting (modifying tasks, relationships, or meaning-making at work) can be deliberately shaped by how organisations frame AI introduction; deliberately managing cognitive appraisal during AI rollout may increase employee proactivity rather than defensiveness.

Understanding whether employees perceive AI as a stressor or resource determines downstream behaviours; tailor change communication and support to shift appraisal from threat-focused (stress) toward challenge-focused (growth opportunity).

articles.title: The impact of generative AI use on employees’ psychological distress: a moderated mediation model - Frontiers
articles.snippet: The impact of generative AI use on employees’ psychological distress: a moderated mediation model  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Limited generalisability without access to full methodology. The study's scope, sample size, geographic location, and sector focus are unclear from the title and snippet alone, making it difficult to assess how broadly findings apply to other employee populations.
takeaways: Generative AI adoption can trigger psychological distress in employees — identify and monitor key stressors (skill gaps, role uncertainty, workload shifts) during implementation to target support proactively.

The moderated mediation model suggests distress pathways are conditional — tailor change management strategies by mapping which employee groups or contexts face highest risk, then adjust communication, training, or role adjustments accordingly.

Early intervention during AI rollout (before distress escalates) is likely more cost-effective than remedial support — design onboarding and upskilling programmes that explicitly address anxiety and uncertainty about AI's impact on jobs.

topics.label: Fascinating Psychology Research
topics.description: Surprising, counterintuitive, and delightful findings from personality and behaviour research — the kind of study you'd share at dinner.

articles.title: Brain scans reveal a shocking difference between psychopaths and other people - Science Daily
articles.snippet: Brain scans reveal a shocking difference between psychopaths and other people  Science Daily
articles.generalisability: Limited — headline-style news report with no detail on study methodology, sample size, or geographic scope. Actual research findings may be more nuanced than the sensationalised title suggests.
takeaways: Psychopathy appears to involve detectable neurobiological differences visible on brain imaging, not just behavioural traits — suggesting it has a measurable physical basis.
The 'shocking difference' framing is typical of science communication; the actual finding is likely more subtle and interesting to neuroscience specialists than the headline implies.
Brain imaging studies can reveal structural or functional oddities, but correlation between scans and behaviour doesn't prove causation — a reminder to be sceptical of dramatic brain-science claims.

articles.title: New psychology research shows the surprising romantic advantage of antagonistic narcissism - PsyPost
articles.snippet: New psychology research shows the surprising romantic advantage of antagonistic narcissism  PsyPost
articles.generalisability: Limited — based on a single psychology study; geographic scope and sample characteristics not clear from snippet alone.
takeaways: Counterintuitively, antagonistic narcissism (dominance-seeking, combative traits) may paradoxically boost romantic success in short-term contexts, contradicting the intuition that narcissism is universally off-putting.
The finding highlights a puzzling mismatch between what people say they want in partners (warmth, reliability) and what some personality traits actually deliver in attracting romantic interest.

This touches on a broader tension in evolutionary psychology: traits that seem socially costly (like antagonism) sometimes confer mating advantages under specific circumstances, making human attraction more complex than personality tests suggest.

articles.title: When personality meets surprise: individual differences in memory for unexpected events - Frontiers
articles.snippet: When personality meets surprise: individual differences in memory for unexpected events  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Unclear from snippet alone — sample size, geographic scope, and participant demographics not provided in the available information.
takeaways: People with different personality traits remember surprising or unexpected events in systematically different ways — meaning personality isn't just about how you act, it's also about what your brain chooses to hold onto.

This suggests that eyewitness accounts of the same surprising event will vary not just because people were paying different attention, but because their fundamental personality shapes what they encode into memory in the first place.
The finding is counterintuitive because we often assume memory for shocking or unexpected moments would be equally vivid across people — but personality appears to act as a filter on what sticks.

articles.title: How a twin study untangled the surprising roots of authoritarian political beliefs - PsyPost
articles.snippet: How a twin study untangled the surprising roots of authoritarian political beliefs  PsyPost
articles.generalisability: Findings from twin studies are generally limited to populations similar to the sample studied; geographic scope and sample characteristics are not detailed in the snippet, so applicability beyond the study population is unclear.
takeaways: Twin studies reveal that authoritarian political beliefs have a significant genetic component — suggesting personality and temperament, not just environment or media exposure, shape how people relate to authority.

The 'nature vs. nurture' split on authoritarianism is more nuanced than assumed — both inherited traits and life experiences matter, which explains why identical twins can still end up with different political leanings.

This finding is counterintuitive because authoritarianism is often framed as purely ideological or socially learned, when in fact individual differences in how people process hierarchy and order appear wired in from the start.

articles.title: Musical preferences unite personalities across the globe - University of Cambridge
articles.snippet: Musical preferences unite personalities across the globe  University of Cambridge
articles.generalisability: High — findings appear to span multiple countries and cultures, suggesting universal patterns in how personality traits relate to music taste.
takeaways: Your music taste really does reflect your personality in consistent ways across different cultures — suggesting that preference for, say, jazz or heavy metal reveals something fundamentally human rather than purely cultural.

Personality-music links are surprisingly universal despite vast cultural differences in which genres exist and flourish locally — a counterintuitive finding that hints at deeper psychological drivers of aesthetic choice.

This opens a fun party trick: personality psychologists might predict what someone enjoys listening to better than you'd expect, based purely on psychological traits like openness to experience or conscientiousness.

articles.title: An AI analyzed wine reviews and found a surprising link to personality - PsyPost
articles.snippet: An AI analyzed wine reviews and found a surprising link to personality  PsyPost
articles.generalisability: Limited — article snippet is too brief to assess sample size, methodology, or geographic scope. Full study details needed to evaluate generalisability.
takeaways: Wine preferences reveal personality traits — the AI found personality patterns embedded in how people write about wine, suggesting our taste in beverages might be a window into who we are.
Language analysis can infer personality — this study shows AI can extract psychological insights from everyday writing, even on seemingly trivial topics like wine reviews.

The surprising angle: most people wouldn't expect their casual wine tasting notes to betray their deeper personality — yet the data suggests otherwise, making this both fun and a bit creepy in equal measure.

topics.label: Psychological Safety
topics.description: Research on psychological safety and its role in team learning, AI experimentation, and innovation.

articles.title: The dark side of artificial intelligence adoption: linking artificial intelligence adoption to employee depression via psychological safety and ethical leadership | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications - Nature
articles.snippet: The dark side of artificial intelligence adoption: linking artificial intelligence adoption to employee depression via psychological safety and ethical leadership | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications  Nature
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on sample composition and size, which are not evident from the title and snippet. The causal pathways between AI adoption, psychological safety, ethical leadership, and depression warrant replication across different organisational contexts and geographies before broad application.
takeaways: AI adoption can harm employee mental health if organisations fail to maintain psychological safety — leaders must actively protect employees' sense of safety, voice, and belonging during technological transitions, not assume these needs diminish with automation.

Ethical leadership is a critical moderator: leaders who model integrity, transparency, and concern for employee welfare during AI implementation can buffer negative psychological effects, whereas purely technocratic or opaque rollouts increase depression risk.

When planning AI capability development, assess and monitor psychological safety metrics alongside adoption metrics; employee depression and disengagement may signal deeper concerns about fairness, job security, or change management rather than resistance to the technology itself.

articles.title: Team Dynamics Weaken When Employees Turn to AI Instead of Colleagues - Harvard Business Review
articles.snippet: Team Dynamics Weaken When Employees Turn to AI Instead of Colleagues  Harvard Business Review
articles.generalisability: Limited — presents a conceptual argument without empirical data or specific organizational context. The claim requires validation through controlled studies across different team types and industries before broad application.
takeaways: Monitor whether AI adoption is reducing peer-to-peer interactions on your teams; create explicit norms that preserve colleague collaboration for complex problem-solving and relationship-building, rather than defaulting to AI for all queries.

When introducing AI tools, frame them as supplements to team dialogue rather than replacements — e.g., use AI for preliminary research, then discuss findings as a group to maintain psychological safety and trust.

Watch for 'AI silos' where individuals solve problems independently via AI and disengage from collective sense-making; schedule regular team check-ins to surface challenges and decisions that benefit from shared reasoning.

articles.title: Psychological Safety Levels the Playing Field for Employees - Boston Consulting Group
articles.snippet: Psychological Safety Levels the Playing Field for Employees  Boston Consulting Group
articles.generalisability: Moderate — BCG's insights are based on consulting experience across multiple sectors and geographies, but specific methodological details, sample characteristics, and whether findings are primarily US-focused are unclear from the snippet alone.
takeaways: Create explicit norms and practices that invite quieter or marginalised team members to contribute equally — psychological safety reduces barriers to voice and participation, levelling influence across hierarchy and demographic differences.

Measure psychological safety alongside other team health metrics to identify where employees feel unsafe speaking up, then address specific blockers (e.g. fear of embarrassment, punitive responses) rather than assuming one-size-fits-all interventions will work.

Model vulnerability and non-defensiveness as a leader — acknowledging your own mistakes and uncertainty signals that failure and dissent are safe, which is foundational to creating genuine psychological safety rather than surface-level 'openness.'

articles.title: Global Workforce Hopes and Fears Survey 2026 - PwC
articles.snippet: Global Workforce Hopes and Fears Survey 2026  PwC
articles.generalisability: Moderate to high — PwC's global workforce surveys typically reach thousands of respondents across multiple countries and sectors, though specific sample composition and methodology are not detailed in the snippet provided.
takeaways: Use PwC's findings on workforce concerns to conduct a listening session with your teams — identify which 'fears' resonate locally and address them through transparent communication and involvement in decision-making, which are key drivers of psychological safety.

Map the survey's 'hopes' against your organisation's AI capability development strategy; misalignment between what employees want (e.g., upskilling, job security) and what you're offering creates safety risks — proactively communicate how AI investment protects roles and creates growth.

If the survey highlights anxiety about AI adoption, use the data to make the business case for psychological safety initiatives — showing leadership that unaddressed workforce concerns directly impact adoption risk and retention.

articles.title: The work affective well-being under the impact of AI - Nature
articles.snippet: The work affective well-being under the impact of AI  Nature
articles.generalisability: Cannot be fully assessed from the title and snippet alone, but Nature publications typically have rigorous methodology. Geographic scope and sample characteristics would need to be reviewed in the full article to determine applicability to Australian workplace contexts.
takeaways: Monitor and measure employee emotional well-being and mood in your workplace as AI adoption increases — affective states may shift in ways that affect psychological safety and team dynamics.
Create safe spaces for staff to discuss anxieties or concerns about AI implementation; unaddressed emotional reactions can undermine both psychological safety and acceptance of new tools.
Design AI rollout processes that protect workers' sense of control and autonomy, as threats to these may negatively impact affective well-being and erode psychological safety.

articles.title: Fostering Ethical Conduct Through Psychological Safety - MIT Sloan Management Review
articles.snippet: Fostering Ethical Conduct Through Psychological Safety  MIT Sloan Management Review
articles.generalisability: Moderate — presents conceptual framework linking psychological safety to ethical conduct, but lacks empirical data on implementation scope or sector applicability. Generalisability depends on organisational context and culture.
takeaways: Create explicit psychological safety norms around ethical dilemmas and speaking up about misconduct — employees are more likely to report concerns and challenge unethical decisions when they trust they won't face retribution.

Leaders should model vulnerability and admit mistakes publicly; this signals that psychological safety extends to ethical reasoning, not just operational risk-taking, encouraging team members to raise ethical concerns early.

Audit your current feedback and reporting mechanisms to ensure they genuinely protect psychologically safe voice — anonymous channels alone are insufficient if employees fear informal consequences or career impact.
